content: Zidovudine, when taken orally, can reduce the number of certain white blood cells in the body, potentially leading to anemia and muscle disorders. It may also cause severe liver damage and a condition known as lactic acidosis, especially when used alone or in combination with other antiviral medications. If you experience symptoms such as stomach upset, loss of appetite, dark yellow or brown urine, unusual bleeding or bruising, flu-like symptoms, yellowing of the skin or eyes, pain in the upper right part of your stomach, muscle weakness, lack of strength, muscle pain, shortness of breath, unusual tiredness or weakness, or pale skin, contact your doctor immediately. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as your doctor will monitor your response to zidovudine through specific lab tests. Zidovudine is prescribed to treat human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection in patients with or without acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It works by slowing the spread of HIV in the body. However, it is not a cure for HIV and may not reduce the number of HIV-related illnesses. Zidovudine does not prevent the transmission of HIV to others, except when administered to HIV-positive pregnant women to reduce the risk of passing the infection to their baby. Despite this treatment, HIV infection may still occur in the infant. Zidovudine may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Zidovudine is available as capsules, tablets, and syrup for oral use. It is typically taken three to four times a day, and in some cases, up to five times a day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take zidovudine exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed. Continue taking zidovudine even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Zidovudine is sometimes used to treat healthcare workers and others exposed to HIV infection after accidental contact with HIV-contaminated blood, tissues, or other body fluids. Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Before taking zidovudine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to zidovudine or any other drugs. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially acetaminophen, acyclovir (Zovirax), aspirin, cimetidine (Tagamet), fluconazole (Diflucan), foscarnet (Foscavir), ganciclovir (Cytovene), indomethacin (Indocin), interferon, lorazepam (Ativan), oxazepam (Serax), probenecid (Benemid), valproic acid (Depakene, Depakote), and vitamins. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had liver or kidney disease, muscle disorders or swelling, anemia, a history of alcohol abuse, or bleeding or other blood problems. Let your doctor know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking zidovudine, contact your doctor. Additionally, inform your doctor if you consume alcohol. Zidovudine should be taken at least 30 minutes before or 1 hour after a meal. Take it while sitting up and with plenty of water. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Mild side effects of zidovudine are common. Notify your doctor if any of these symptoms are severe or persistent: stomach pain, diarrhea or loose stools, constipation, headache, dizziness, or difficulty sleeping. If you experience a rash or any of the symptoms listed in the Important Warning section, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects should be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store zidovudine in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of outdated or no longer needed medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the victim has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Do not share your medication with anyone else. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
